name: Sara Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on Ward 6, general medicine, at the district hospital in our town. Mostly older patients with chest infections, falls, heart failure, that sort of thing. A day shift is twelve and a half hours: handover at quarter past seven, drug round, washes, obs (that's blood pressure, pulse, temperature), then dressings, discharges and admissions all landing at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the patients, honestly, the old men who tell you about the war their dad was in, the ladies who want their hair done before visiting. What wears me out is being one nurse to nine or ten patients and still being slow at things like IV drug sums. Ruth, our charge nurse, checks my work a lot, and she's right to, but I go home feeling like I'm always behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most promises the hospital makes. Lots of noise, a new screen, and the ward stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the staff room: good, now can we talk about staffing. A gadget that saves ten minutes doesn't help when we're two nurses short on a Saturday night. I'd probably share some union post about it and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, because I'm not good with new systems. But relieved doesn't mean okay. I still earn the bottom of the pay band, Tom and I still split the rent on the flat above the bakery, and I've got maybe three weeks of money if anything goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep my head down, and try to pass my IV competency sign-off before spring. I'd go to the union meeting about the new rota, because that matters more to me than any AI. And I'd still be checking the bank app before I buy anything bigger than a sandwich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear, it's that slow grind where nothing gets better and nothing gets worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three weeks of money. What happens if something goes wrong in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the car's clutch went and I had to borrow from my mum to fix it. She's on a pension, so I hated asking. If it happened again I'd probably skip the car and get the early bus, which means leaving at half five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk, Denise, maybe, if the computer starts doing her booking and letters. She's the one who actually knows where everything is. Nurses would be fine, we'd just be tired like always.

say: A small time saver is **fine**, but our real problem is **staffing**, not software.
I'd share the **union's line** that wards need nurses, not gadgets.
think: I'm **relieved**, because I struggle with new computer systems and dread every update.
My **thin savings** and **low pay** still leave me one broken car away from trouble.
do: Keep working my **day shifts** and pass the **IV competency** sign-off before spring.
Go to the **union meeting** about the new rota instead of worrying about AI.
Keep checking the **bank app** before any purchase bigger than lunch.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, stuck in a grind where nothing improves.
S0.quote: A gadget that saves ten minutes doesn't help when we're two nurses short on a Saturday night.
fieldNote: Her mind goes straight to **staffing** and the rota, not to the technology.
She admits she is **bad with new systems**, which makes a quiet plateau a relief.
Money pressure is real: **three weeks** of savings and a past loan from her **mum**.

steps.text: Pass the IV drug competency sign-off on Ward 6 before spring
Attend the union meeting about the new ward rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds more real to me. The thinking stuff gets taken over, and somebody decides what counts as thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be the one saying nurses aren't robots and patients aren't spreadsheets. I'd push for the union to get a say before any of it comes on the ward. If the hospital tries to use it to cut the number of nurses per shift, I'd be at the protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared of the charting part. The care plans, the risk scores, the handover notes would all go to some system, and I'm the slowest on the computers on Ward 6. And Tom drives the number 12 bus, which I think is more at risk than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's working group on new technology, even though I hate computers, because I want a nurse like me in the room. I'd cut the takeaway nights and the streaming subscriptions to put fifty a month aside. And I'd make Tom look at what training the bus company offers before they need fewer drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm being pushed somewhere I didn't choose. I trained to look after people, not to look after a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day do you think changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork side. Admissions forms, the falls risk score, the fluid charts, the discharge letters. If the machine fills those in and I have to check them, I'll be checking something I don't fully understand, and I'll be the one who signs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tom's job worries you more than yours. What would that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Tom lost the bus job we'd be on my wage alone, and my wage doesn't cover the rent and the car. We'd have to move somewhere cheaper, and there isn't really cheaper in our town. I'd probably pick up extra bank shifts, which means even less time together.

say: I'd say **patients aren't spreadsheets**, and nurses should have a **say** before new systems arrive.
I'd join a **protest** if the hospital used AI to cut **nurses per shift**.
think: I'm the **slowest on computers** on the ward, so AI charting scares me.
Tom's **bus driving job** looks more at risk than my nursing job.
do: Join the union's **technology working group** so a junior nurse is in the room.
Cut takeaways and streaming to save **fifty a month**.
Push Tom to ask the bus company about **retraining** before cuts come.
feel: **Pushed** somewhere she didn't choose, caring for a tablet instead of people.
S1.quote: I trained to look after people, not to look after a tablet.
fieldNote: She frames AI as a **workload and staffing** fight, not a technology question.
Her real fear is being **accountable** for AI paperwork she can't check well.
The household risk sits with her partner's **bus job**, not her own.

steps.text: Join the union's working group on new ward technology
Cancel two streaming subscriptions and takeaway nights to save fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before I've even finished my preceptorship booklet. That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in now, not after. Rules on what AI can sign off, a guarantee on nurse numbers, and proper support for people like Tom who lose their jobs. I'd be posting that everywhere, and I'd be at the town hall if there was a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the paperwork side of my job is gone by 2028, and then the hospital decides it needs fewer nurses per ward. The hands-on care lasts until robots come, so maybe 2031, but I'm junior and not the best, so I'd be the first one they don't need. And by then Tom's bus could be driving itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every union action going and write to our MP about safe staffing laws. I'd cut back to the bone: sell the car, take the bus, stop the gym. And I'd ask my mum whether Tom and I could move back in with her if it came to it, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor's going and I'm not quick enough to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tom the night you heard about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom we need a plan B that isn't the bus or the ward. Then I'd probably cry, because I don't have a plan B, I only have nursing. He'd say we'll be fine, he always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a bit, because someone still has to turn patients and hold hands until 2031. But three years isn't long when you're on the lowest pay band with no savings. It means I lose the paperwork part first and then the rest.

say: The **government** must act now with **safe staffing** laws and limits on what AI signs off.
People who lose work, like Tom on the **buses**, need real **support**.
think: The **paperwork** side of nursing goes by **2028**, then wards need fewer nurses.
As a **junior** and not the best, I'd be first to go when robots arrive.
do: Join every **union action** and write to our **MP** about safe staffing laws.
**Sell the car** and drop the gym to cut costs right away.
Ask Mum if we could **move back in** with her if needed.
feel: **Sick** and frightened, like the floor is going and she's too slow to jump.
S2.quote: Two years? That's before I've even finished my preceptorship booklet.
fieldNote: The short timeline hits her **career stage** hard: she hasn't finished basic training.
She sees the **three-year gap** before robots as delay, not safety.
She leans on **politics** and her **mum**, not on learning the tools.

steps.text: Join every union action for safe staffing on wards
Write to the local MP asking for safe staffing laws
Sell the car and take the early bus to the hospital
Ask Mum about moving back in with Tom if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast. But at least you'd see it coming, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but louder: we've got five years, so use them. Make the hospitals sign agreements on nurse numbers now. I'd want the union to be negotiating, not just shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be thirty-two when it lands, with the robots at thirty-five. That's enough time to get good at the job, which I'm not yet. But I know myself, I'd probably spend the first two years hoping it wasn't true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on Ward 6 and actually get my competencies done, so I'm not the weakest when cuts come. I'd try to save something every month, even forty, in a separate account I can't see. And I'd stay active in the union and vote for whoever promises safe staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like a long knot in my stomach than panic. I hate that AGI is coming. Five years just gives me more time to hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend two years hoping it wasn't true. Is that what you'd actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'm not proud of it. Ruth would tell me to get on with the training and I'd say yes and then not do it until somebody made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to save that forty a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday takeaway with Tom, and the phone contract, I'd go to a cheaper one. It doesn't sound like much, but I've never had forty spare at the end of a month.

say: We have **five years**, so unions should negotiate **nurse numbers** now, not just shout.
Hospitals should sign **agreements** before the new systems arrive.
think: I'd be **thirty-two** when AGI lands and thirty-five when robots come.
I'd probably spend **two years** hoping it wasn't true before acting.
do: Finish my **ward competencies** so I'm not the weakest when cuts come.
Save **forty a month** in a separate account by dropping takeaway and switching phone plans.
Stay active in the **union** and vote for safe staffing.
feel: A long **knot** in her stomach rather than panic, with time to dread it.
S3.quote: I hate that AGI is coming. Five years just gives me more time to hate it.
fieldNote: She is honest about her own **avoidance**: she'd delay acting.
Five years still feels **too short** for a junior on low pay with no savings.
She would back **negotiation** over protest when there is more time.

steps.text: Save forty a month in a separate account she can't see
Push the union to negotiate nurse numbers with the hospital
Vote for candidates who promise safe staffing laws

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That one I can almost breathe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly, with nurses at the table. Train people, protect the wards, don't let the hospital board use it to save money. I'd still be in the union saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when the robots come. By then I'd hope to be a proper experienced nurse, maybe a senior one. I hate AGI coming, but ten years means I might be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and get good at the job, that's the main thing. I'd save what I can, maybe put Tom and me on a plan to have two months' rent by the end of next year. I'd keep going to union meetings and I'd let them do the technology side while I do the patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, still. It's not my world anymore at the end, but there's time to make some peace with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the union handle the technology side. Is there any part you'd learn yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the basics, if they made it part of mandatory training. I wouldn't go looking for it. I'd rather learn to put a cannula in first time than learn to talk to a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough for Tom to switch to something else, maybe a mechanic course. He's good with engines. I'd nag him about it every birthday.

say: Ten years is enough to do it **properly**, with nurses **at the table**.
The hospital board shouldn't use AI just to **save money** on wards.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** at AGI and forty when robots arrive.
With ten years, I could be the **experienced nurse** they keep.
do: Stay on the ward and get **good at the job**, cannulas first.
Build **two months' rent** in savings with Tom by the end of next year.
Keep going to **union meetings** and leave the technology side to them.
feel: Still **uneasy**, but with time to make **peace** with it.
S4.quote: I'd rather learn to put a cannula in first time than learn to talk to a computer.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her from **alarmed** to **steadier**, but money still bites.
She still **won't seek out** AI tools, only mandatory training.
Her plan rests on becoming **experienced** before the robots come.

steps.text: Practise cannulas until she gets them in first time
Build two months' rent in savings with Tom by next year
Keep attending union meetings on new ward technology

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Because I'm junior, I'm slow on computers and we've got no savings, and Tom's job goes too. What would help is a law on safe nurse numbers, and some real money for people retraining, so Tom and I aren't moving back into my mum's spare room at thirty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the hospital itself. Everybody talks about AI like it's the big threat, but I've watched three nurses leave Ward 6 this year because of burnout. If the hospital fixed that first, I'd be a lot less scared of AI.

headlineQuote: I've watched three nurses leave Ward 6 this year because of burnout. If the hospital fixed that first, I'd be a lot less scared of AI.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior nurse on a general medicine ward in a small town, still learning her **IV drug sums**.
She rents with Tom, a **bus driver**, and has about **three weeks** of savings.
She avoids new technology and turns every scenario into a fight about **staffing** and the **union**.
Her mood moves from **uneasy** in the plateau to **alarmed** when AGI comes fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she's junior, slow on computers, and Tom's bus job goes too.
whatWouldHelp: A law on **safe nurse numbers** and real **retraining** money for people like Tom.
